0.title: How to Behave in the Household of God
0.overview:
First Timothy is a letter from a seasoned apostle to a young pastor — and it is as practical and urgent as anything Paul ever wrote. Timothy had been left in Ephesus to deal with a crisis: false teachers were infecting the church with 'different doctrine,' with myths and endless genealogies, with a distorted use of the law and a spiritualised asceticism that forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul's letter is his pastoral briefing for a young man who has been given a very hard assignment in a very important city.

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia — a commercial and religious metropolis, home to the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. It was a city Paul knew intimately: he had spent nearly three years there on his third missionary journey (Acts 19–20), and the church he planted was one of the most strategic in the Roman East. Now, years later, that church was in danger. The false teachers were not outsiders; they had come from within — perhaps former elders or teachers who had 'made shipwreck of their faith' (1:19–20). Timothy's task was to confront them, silence them, and restore the church to sound doctrine and ordered life.

The letter's great themes weave together seamlessly. There is the primacy of sound doctrine — 'the glorious gospel of the blessed God' (1:11) — against which every false teaching must be measured. There is the ordering of the church: prayer, worship, the qualifications of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, the honour due to elders. There is the call to godliness — a word that appears more often in 1 Timothy than in any other New Testament letter — the practical Christlikeness that is the goal of all authentic teaching. And there are the five 'trustworthy sayings' (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Tit 3:8) — compact theological summaries that sound like early confessions of faith, already familiar in the church before Paul wrote them down.

Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters? Many scholars think a later follower wrote them in his name, arguing that their vocabulary and style differ from Paul’s other letters, that their church order with elders and deacons looks later, and that their travels cannot be fitted into Acts. But each letter names Paul as author, they were received as his by the early church, and the church order they describe is simple: plural elders and deacons, which Paul appointed from his first journey (Acts 14:23; Phil 1:1). Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to trusted co-workers on new subjects. And the travels fit if Paul was released from the imprisonment with which Acts ends, as the early church believed, and then travelled again, to Macedonia (1:3), Crete (Titus 1:5) and elsewhere, before a final arrest. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote them, in the mid-60s.

And what was Timothy’s role? Not a bishop of Ephesus in the later sense, but Paul’s delegate, sent with apostolic authority for a time, Until I come (4:13), to correct false teaching and see that qualified elders led the church (3:1–7; 5:17–22).

Above all, this is a letter about the church as 'the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth' (3:15). The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is the family of the living God, called to hold up the truth in a world drowning in falsehood. That is what gives urgency to every instruction about doctrine and order and godliness: the stakes are not institutional but cosmic. The household of God must be governed well — because the God who indwells it is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords (6:15).

1.title: The Glorious Gospel and the Worst of Sinners
1.overview:
Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain men teaching a different doctrine: myths, genealogies and confident talk about the law that produced endless speculation instead of love. The law is good, Paul says, when used for its purpose: to convict sinners, measured by the gospel of God’s glory.

Then Paul turns to himself as the proof of that gospel. He had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man, and Christ showed him mercy. “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” If Christ’s patience reached him, it can reach anyone, and the thought breaks into praise. The chapter ends with a charge to Timothy to fight the good fight, keeping faith and a good conscience, unlike two men who wrecked their faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, an apostle by the command of God our Saviour and of Christ Jesus our hope, writes to Timothy, his true son in the faith: grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Our Saviour, and Mercy Added

The Pastorals call the Father ‘Saviour’ — salvation was his design, as the Son accomplished it — and only the letters to Timothy add ‘mercy’ to grace and peace: compassion for a struggling minister.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young, unwarlike Timothy (4:12; 2 Tim 1:7) needed the apostolic commission standing behind him.

Now: ‘Christ Jesus our hope’ tells anyone in a hard post where to look when the situation offers nothing to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Saviour and of Christ Jesus our hope, writes to Timothy, his true son in the faith: grace, mercy and peace.

By command. Epitagē, a royal order. Paul did not volunteer. For a young, unwarlike Timothy (4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7), facing men who did not want him, the chain of command runs above them both.

God our Saviour. The Pastorals call the Father Saviour (2:3; 4:10): salvation was his design, accomplished by the Son. In Ephesus, emperors and Artemis claimed the title.

Our hope. Future-facing: where to look in a post that will not get easier soon.

True child. Gnēsios, legitimately born, genuine, against the would-be teachers of v. 7.

Mercy. Only in the letters to Timothy. Grace is favour to the undeserving; mercy is compassion for the struggling. God’s attitude to a tired minister is not measured by how well he is coping.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a hard place you did not choose, the One who sent you is above everyone who resents you.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and joined Paul on his second journey. The letter seems to come from after the events of Acts, probably after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, in the early to mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No thanksgiving: Paul goes straight to the problem. Timothy must stay in Ephesus and order certain people to stop teaching a different doctrine, and to stop devoting themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which produce speculation rather than God’s work, which is by faith. The goal is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. Some have wandered from this into empty talk, wanting to be teachers of the law without understanding it. The law is good when used properly: not for the righteous, but for the lawless, the ungodly, those who kill their parents, murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practise homosexuality, slave traders, liars and perjurers, and anything else contrary to the sound teaching of the gospel of God’s glory entrusted to Paul.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Teaching Is For

The telos of the whole charge is love (v.5) — Paul is not setting doctrine against love but saying what doctrine is for — and the law, good when used lawfully (v.8), convicts sinners and drives them to Christ rather than feeding speculation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul diagnoses the Ephesian teaching by its output — endless speculation rather than God's household well run (v.4).

Now: The vice list of vv.9–10 must be read where Paul put it: five verses before he calls himself the foremost sinner alive.

verseByVerse.quote: As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As I urged you when I left for Macedonia, stay in Ephesus so that you can instruct certain people not to teach false doctrine, and not to give themselves to myths and endless genealogies. These promote speculation rather than God’s work, which is done by faith.

No thanksgiving. The omission measures how serious things were.

Remain. Asked twice. Timothy probably wanted to leave. Scripture records it without embarrassment.

Different doctrine. Heterodidaskalein: teaching of another kind from what was handed down.

Myths and genealogies. Probably speculative Jewish elaboration of Old Testament family lists. Paul does not describe it; he judges it by its output.

Speculation or stewardship. Open-ended talk that never lands, against oikonomia, the ordered running of God’s household. The test: does this teaching produce endless discussion, or does it get God’s house run?

A textual note. Some manuscripts read oikodomē, “edifying” (KJV “godly edifying”). Oikonomia, “stewardship”, is far better attested. The point is similar either way.

On a Tuesday. Beware subjects designed never to conclude. They make you feel sophisticated and never require you to do anything.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, where Paul had spent about three years.

verseByVerse.quote: The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of this instruction is love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience and a sincere faith.

The aim. Telos: the point of the whole exercise. Not correct opinions or defeated opponents, but love.

What it does not mean. Not doctrine against love. Six chapters of doctrine and order follow. Paul says what doctrine is for. Theology that does not arrive here has failed on its own terms.

Three sources, three counterfeits blocked. A pure heart: without it, love becomes a performance. A good conscience: without it, love becomes the busy kindness of someone avoiding something. Sincere faith, un-masked: without it, love becomes correct behaviour from someone who does not trust God.

On a Tuesday. Ask of the teaching you consume and the arguments you join: what does this grow in me?

verseByVerse.quote: Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some have turned away from these and wandered into empty talk. They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or the things they insist on so confidently.

Swerving. Astocheō: an archer missing the mark. Not enemies from outside, but church people who aimed and went wide. That can happen to anyone who stops checking where he is pointing.

Empty talk. Not necessarily false, but empty: heat without content.

Desire first. They wanted to be teachers, then found a subject. The reverse of how it should be.

Confident ignorance. Certainty without comprehension is the signature. Real understanding usually makes people more careful.

On a Tuesday. Want to teach? First want to understand.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that the law is good, if it is used properly.

A pun. Nomos used nomimōs: the law used lawfully.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is the problem. Paul heads off that conclusion, drawn often in church history. The law is God’s and good.

The uses of the law. The Reformed tradition speaks of three: it restrains evil in society; it exposes sin and drives us to Christ (Paul’s point in v. 9); and it guides believers in a life that pleases God. Lutherans stress the second; some others deny the third. The false teachers invented a fourth: raw material for speculation.

Misuse, not disuse. When something good is handled badly, the instinct is to stop teaching it. Paul explains what it is for. The cure for bad use is good use.

verseByVerse.quote: understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is not made for righteous people, but for the lawless and rebellious, the ungodly and sinful, the unholy and irreligious, for those who kill their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practise homosexuality, slave traders, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound teaching.

Not for the just. The law as accuser has nothing to say to someone already doing what it requires. Warning notices are for those inclined to the act.

The Ten Commandments. The list follows them: first the God-ward failures, then parents (fifth), murder (sixth), sexual sin (seventh), slave-trading as the worst theft (eighth), lying and perjury (ninth).

Men who practise homosexuality. Arsenokoitai, built from the Greek of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. Attempts to narrow it to exploitation have to work against that origin. The historic Christian reading is the plain one.

Where Paul put it. Beside liars and men who strike their parents, five verses before he calls himself the foremost sinner. Any use of this verse that leaves the reader feeling superior has misread it. The same gospel offers washing to all (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

Enslavers. Kidnappers and slave traders, condemned inside an empire built on slavery.

Sound. Healthy teaching. Everything on this list makes people ill.
verseByVerse.note: The list follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from the first table (God) to the second (neighbour).

verseByVerse.quote: in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which has been entrusted to me.

The gospel of the glory. Not only a glorious gospel, but a gospel whose content is God’s glory.

The blessed God. Makarios, the Beatitudes’ word. God is perfectly, self-sufficiently happy. He did not save out of loneliness or lack; the gospel is the overflow of his fullness.

The measure. Paul does not refute the teachers point by point. He holds them up against this and lets the mismatch speak.

Entrusted. A deposit (6:20). Paul did not devise or own the message. That is the only safe posture for correcting anyone’s doctrine.

For worship. The God who needs nothing gave everything.

verseByVerse.ref: 1:12–17 – Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and trusting him with ministry, although he had been a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man. He received mercy because he acted in ignorance and unbelief, and the Lord’s grace overflowed to him, with faith and love. The saying is trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul is the worst. He was shown mercy so that Christ could display his perfect patience in him as an example for all who would believe. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honour and glory for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Present Tense of Verse 15

‘Of whom I am the foremost’ — not was. Nearness to light shows more dust, not less, and only a man who sees himself so can correct others without contempt.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The persecutor became the pattern (v.16): Christ's patience with him is the outer limit that no later case exceeds.

Now: The doxology of verse 17 comes from a man remembering his own conversion and unable to finish the sentence without worship.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has given me strength, that he considered me trustworthy and appointed me to serve him, even though I was once a blasphemer, a persecutor and a violent man. But I was shown mercy because I acted in ignorance and unbelief, and the grace of our Lord poured out on me abundantly, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

Judged me faithful. Extraordinary, and Paul says why.

Three words. Blasphemer (he tried to make others curse Christ, Acts 26:11). Persecutor (house to house, Acts 8:3). Hybristēs: the violent man who enjoys humiliating people. The ugliest, chosen about himself.

Ignorantly. Not an excuse. The law distinguished unwitting sins from defiant ones (Numbers 15:30). Paul was catastrophically, sincerely wrong: not innocent, but reachable.

Overflowed. Hyperepleonasen, super-abounded. Where sin was extreme, grace was more so.

With faith and love. Not his contribution; they came in the flood. Here is where the love of v. 5 comes from.

On a Tuesday. No one you are praying for is further gone than Saul of Tarsus was.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This saying is trustworthy and deserves to be fully accepted: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and I am the worst of them.

A trustworthy saying. The first of five (3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8): probably a line the churches already said or sang.

Nine words. Came into the world: he existed before. To save: purpose. Sinners: not the promising or nearly good.

I am. Present tense, decades into his apostleship. Not false humility. Nearness to light shows more dust, not less. Growth does not mean an improving opinion of ourselves.

How it functions. Paul is about to discipline two men (v. 20). Only someone who genuinely thinks himself the foremost sinner can correct others without contempt.

For worship. This sentence has been the doorway into faith for countless people who thought they were too bad. It is meant to be.
verseByVerse.note: The first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters.

verseByVerse.quote: But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I was shown mercy for this reason: so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus could display his perfect patience as an example for those who would believe in him and receive eternal life. Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

An exhibit. Hypotypōsis, a pattern-sketch. Paul’s conversion was a demonstration.

The outer limit. If Christ’s patience reached a man who hunted his people, nobody after can say their case is too hard. The worst case on record was received.

Patience. Makrothymia, long-tempered, for all the years Saul did his worst.

The doxology. King of the ages: he rules this era too. Immortal: unlike all Timothy faced. Invisible: the pastoral difficulty, since the opposition is very visible. The only God: a stand in Artemis’s city.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “the only wise God” (KJV), probably from Romans 16:27. “The only God” is earlier.

For worship. Paul remembers his conversion and cannot finish the sentence without praise. That tests whether the gospel has been understood or merely learned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul entrusts this charge to Timothy, in keeping with the prophecies once made about him, so that he may fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience. Some have rejected conscience and wrecked their faith, including Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan so that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Goes First — Conduct or Doctrine

In verse 19 the conscience goes first and the faith goes down after it; and even the severest discipline, handing over to Satan, is remedial — ‘that they may learn’ (v.20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was to fight by the prophecies once made over him (cf. 4:14).

Now: Shipwreck is what happens when a man keeps sailing while ignoring what his conscience tells him about the rocks.

verseByVerse.quote: This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy, my son, I give you this instruction, in keeping with the prophecies once made about you, so that by remembering them you can fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience. Some have rejected their conscience and so shipwrecked their faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan so that they may learn not to blaspheme.

Entrusted. To Paul (v. 11), now to Timothy. That is how it travels.

The prophecies. Spirit-given words marking Timothy out, probably at his commissioning (4:14). Fight by them: on bad days, remember what was said when you began. Today the church recognises a call by gifts, character and fruit tested by Scripture.

Conscience first. The conscience goes, and faith sinks after it. Not men who reasoned their way out and then lived badly, but men who kept doing what they knew was wrong, until their doctrine followed. Wrong living eventually builds itself a theology.

Lost salvation? Arminian Christians read “shipwreck of their faith” that way. The more likely reading is an outward faith never truly resting on Christ: “if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19).

Handed over to Satan. Put outside the church’s fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:5).

That they may learn. Remedial, not merely punitive (2 Thessalonians 3:15). And “blaspheme” is what Paul once was (v. 13). He hopes for them what happened to him.

On a Tuesday. If your conscience is nagging about one thing, deal with it today. That is how shipwrecks are avoided.
verseByVerse.note: To hand someone “over to Satan” means putting him out of the church, in the hope that he will be brought to repentance.

2.title: One Mediator, Many Prayers
2.overview:
Paul turns to the church’s gathered life. First, prayer for everyone, including rulers such as Nero, because God our Saviour desires all people to be saved, and there is one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. Then conduct in worship: men are to pray without anger or quarrelling; women are to be adorned with good works rather than displays of wealth.

Finally the most debated verses: women are to learn, but not to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, and Paul grounds this in creation, not in Ephesian culture. Here, as throughout, the app holds the complementarian reading, respectfully stated, and insists that a restriction on a role is never a verdict on a person’s worth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: First of all, pray for everyone: requests, prayers, intercessions and thanks, for all people, including kings and those in authority, so that we may live peaceful, quiet lives, godly and dignified. This pleases God our Saviour, who wants all people to be saved and to know the truth. For there is one God and one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony given at the right time. For this Paul was appointed a preacher, apostle and teacher of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
‘Desires All People to Be Saved’

Verse 4 has been read as all kinds of people, or — more often in the Reformed tradition — as God's revealed will set beside his decretive will. Either way there is one mediator, and his ransom is a substitute's (vv.5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Nero, the church was told to pray — and give thanks — for kings (v.2; cf. Jer 29:7).

Now: The aim is modest: a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified. Paul thought that enough to pray for.

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First of all, then, I urge that requests, prayers, intercessions and thanksgiving be made for everyone, for kings and all who are in authority, so that we may live peaceful and quiet lives, godly and dignified in every way.

First, prayer. Not strategy against the opposition, but prayer, and for outsiders.

Four words. Asking from need, general prayer, petition on another’s behalf, and thanks, the surprising one.

Kings. This is Nero’s reign. Pray, and give thanks, for the emperor who would burn Christians and execute Paul. No condition that the ruler deserve it (Romans 13:1; Jeremiah 29:7).

A modest aim. Peace and quiet, room to live well. Smaller than many churches’ ambitions for their nation, and Paul thought it enough.

On a Tuesday. Pray this week, by name, for the leader you like least, and thank God for something he has done.
verseByVerse.note: Christians were to pray for rulers such as Nero, under whom they would later suffer.

parallels.desc: seek the welfare of the city

verseByVerse.quote: This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is good and pleases God our Saviour, who wants all people to be saved and to come to know the truth.

The link. Pray for everyone, because God’s saving concern reaches everyone.

The hard question. If God desires all to be saved, why are not all saved?

Arminian answer. God wants everyone saved and leaves the decision to each person.

Reformed answers. First, the context: “all people” follows kings and rulers (v. 2) and precedes the Gentiles (v. 7), so it may mean all kinds of people. Second, Scripture speaks of God’s will in two ways: his revealed will, what he delights in and commands (he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 33:11), and his decree, what he has purposed to do. God sincerely offers salvation to all and saves those he has chosen. That is the more likely reading.

Common ground. All agree the church must pray for everyone and preach to everyone.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond your prayers: not the magistrate, not the neighbour who reported you.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. This was the testimony given at the right time.

A creed. Compact and balanced; probably a confession the churches used.

One God. The Shema, in a city that chanted “Great is Artemis” for two hours (Acts 19:34).

One mediator. A go-between. Not angels, saints, priests or the church. One point of access, and it is a person.

The man. A mediator needs footing on both sides. Paul presses the human side.

Ransom. Antilytron, a substitute-ransom: he stood where we stood. “Gave himself”: not a reluctant victim.

For all? Some hold that Christ died to make salvation possible for every person. Reformed Christians hold his death is sufficient for all but intended to secure the salvation of his people, reading “all” here as all kinds, as in vv. 1–2. The second is more likely. Both agree the ransom is offered to all and no one who comes is turned away.

For worship. You do not need another go-between. You have him.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this purpose I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

The proof. Paul’s commission to the Gentiles shows God meant “all kinds”.

Three titles. Herald (accurate delivery), apostle (sent with authority), teacher (patient explanation).

Why protest? No one accused him in this sentence. But Gentile inclusion was the fighting ground of his life; he was mobbed for it in Jerusalem (Acts 22:21–22).

Appointed. Set against the men who “desired” to be teachers (1:7). One was placed; the others placed themselves.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts add “in Christ” after “I am telling the truth” (KJV), probably from Romans 9:1. It is not in the earliest copies.

On a Tuesday. Paul did not much mind his reputation. He minded that outsiders were included. Which do you defend more fiercely?

verseByVerse.ref: 2:8–15 – Men and Women in the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Men everywhere should pray, lifting holy hands, without anger or arguing. Women should dress modestly and sensibly, not with elaborate hair, gold, pearls or expensive clothes, but with good works, as is fitting for women who profess godliness. A woman should learn quietly and with submission. Paul does not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man; she is to be quiet. For Adam was formed first, then Eve, and Adam was not deceived; the woman was deceived and fell into sin. Yet she will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Contested Passage, Read Slowly

The crux of verse 12 is authentein; the ESV and the historic Reformed consensus read it as plain authority, restricted rather than abused, and Paul grounds it in the order of creation (vv.13–14) — an order that concerns function, not worth (Gen 1:27; Gal 3:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The braided hair, gold and pearls of verse 9 imported social rank into the assembly; Paul replaces that currency with good works, which nobody can outspend.

Now: Whatever a church concludes about who teaches, a restriction on a function is never a verdict on a person.

verseByVerse.quote: I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or arguing.

The posture. Standing, hands raised and open, the ordinary ancient way of asking. Not a technique; kneeling and bowing are biblical too.

Holy hands. Made unholy not by ritual impurity but by anger and quarrels.

The same track. Worship and relationships run together (Matthew 5:23–24; 1 Peter 3:7). A blockage in one blocks the other.

Everywhere. Not a local Ephesian arrangement, which matters for what follows.

On a Tuesday. Men: if your prayers feel blocked, ask first whether there is someone you are angry with.
verseByVerse.note: Standing with raised hands was a common posture for prayer.

parallels.desc: the lifting up of my hands

verseByVerse.quote: likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, women should dress respectably, with modesty and good sense, not with elaborately braided hair, gold, pearls or expensive clothes, but with good works, as is fitting for women who claim to worship God.

Likewise. Each sex had its besetting problem in that room. Neither instruction is a general verdict on men or women.

The display. Hair braided with gold and pearls took slaves and hours, and announced wealth and rank. The issue is not neatness or a wedding ring but social ranking imported into worship (James 2:1–4).

Modesty and self-control. Not drawing improper attention; settled self-mastery.

With good works. Not “look poor”, but change what you are adorned with. A wealthy woman can outspend a poor one on pearls; nobody can outspend anyone on kindness.

On a Tuesday. Men and women alike: does what you wear on Sunday make the poorest person there feel at home?

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman should learn quietly and with full submission. I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man; she must be quiet.

Let her learn. A command, and generous in a world that rarely educated women religiously. “Submission” is the posture of any learner.

The crux. Authentein, found only here. Egalitarian Christians argue it means “domineer” or “usurp”, so that Paul forbids only abusive authority, or that the restriction was temporary for uneducated women misled in Ephesus. That is a serious view, held by serious Christians.

Why the plain reading is more likely. The word’s use in that period points to ordinary authority. And the two activities joined by “or” must share the same value; since teaching is good throughout these letters, so is having authority. Paul restricts the thing itself, not an abuse of it. And he grounds it in creation (v. 13), not in Ephesian lack of education.

The scope. The gathered church and the office of elder, which requires “the husband of one wife” (3:2). Not silence everywhere: women pray and prophesy (1 Corinthians 11:5); Priscilla helped teach Apollos (Acts 18:26); older women must teach younger (Titus 2:3–4). Churches differ on details such as women teaching mixed groups under the elders’ oversight.

Honestly. Many women live inside this passage and find it costly. It should be handled with care, not triumph.

verseByVerse.quote: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Adam was formed first, then Eve. And Adam was not the one deceived; the woman was deceived and became a sinner.

For. Paul’s grounds decide how far the instruction reaches. He does not appeal to culture or education, which would have limited it to Ephesus. He goes to Genesis.

Order, not worth. Both are made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27); in Christ there is neither male nor female (Galatians 3:28). Order in creation concerns function (compare 1 Corinthians 11:8–9).

What it does not mean. Not that women are more gullible. Paul lays the fall at Adam’s door (Romans 5:12–19). In the garden the serpent went around God’s order; the woman was deceived; Adam, not deceived, went along anyway, which was worse.

On a Tuesday. Whatever a church concludes about who preaches, it settles nothing about the value or gifts of the women in it. If they feel it as a verdict on them, the church has failed to read the rest of the letter.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet she will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love and holiness, with self-control.

What it cannot mean. That women are saved by having babies. There is one mediator (2:5).

Three readings. (1) Saved through the childbirth: the birth of Christ, the woman’s offspring (Genesis 3:15), which fits the garden just mentioned. (2) Kept safe through childbirth, then often fatal. (3) Saved within her ordinary calling, against teachers who forbade marriage (4:3).

The likeliest. The third fits the letter’s argument best: ordinary family life is not an obstacle to salvation but the place it works itself out. The first is attractive and possible.

She, then they. The condition is plural: if they continue.

The anchor. Not if they bear children, but if they continue in faith, love and holiness. What Paul asks of everyone.

For the childless. This verse is no verdict on women who cannot or do not have children. Their salvation rests on the same Christ and shows itself the same way.
verseByVerse.note: One of the harder verses in Paul. Suggested readings include: kept safe through childbirth; saved through the Childbirth, the birth of Christ; or saved while fulfilling her calling. It cannot mean earning salvation.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,<sup>2</sup>for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.<sup>3</sup>This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,<sup>4</sup>who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.<sup>5</sup>For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.<sup>7</sup>For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.<sup>8</sup>I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;<sup>9</sup>likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire,<sup>10</sup>but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.<sup>11</sup>Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness.<sup>12</sup>I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.<sup>13</sup>For Adam was formed first, then Eve;<sup>14</sup>and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.<sup>15</sup>Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

3.title: The Household of God
3.overview:
Paul sets out who may lead God’s household. Overseers (elders) must be men of proven character: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not lovers of money, managing their homes well, mature in faith and respected by outsiders. Only one requirement is a skill: “able to teach”. Deacons, who serve rather than teach, must meet the same standard of character and be tested first.

Then Paul says why it matters. The church is the household of the living God, the pillar that holds up the truth for the world to see. And the truth it holds up is Christ himself, sung in an early hymn: “manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit … taken up in glory.” The rules about wine and money exist so that the pillar stands straight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is a trustworthy saying that whoever aspires to be an overseer desires a good work. An overseer must be above reproach, faithful to his wife, sober, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable and able to teach; not a drunkard or violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money. He must manage his household well, with children who respect him, for if he cannot manage his own household, how can he care for God’s church? He must not be a new convert, or he may become proud and fall as the devil did. And he must have a good reputation with outsiders, so he does not fall into disgrace and the devil’s trap.
verseByVerse.theology:
Character, Not Competence

Of some fifteen requirements only one — ‘able to teach’ — is a skill; everything else concerns what a man is, and the vices named are the kind a congregation cannot see for years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Overseer’ and ‘elder’ name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7).

Now: Verse 7 gives outsiders a say: what would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This saying is trustworthy: anyone who aspires to be an overseer desires a good work.

Aspires. Two positive verbs. Paul does not treat wanting this as suspect, against the idea that the only safe leader is the one dragged to it.

Overseer. Episkopos. The same men are called elders (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7): one office, two names, one from standing, one from function. Episcopal churches see a later distinction between bishops and presbyters; Scripture uses the words together.

A good work. Not a rank or platform. Labour.

Keep the office, raise the bar. Ephesus was full of would-be teachers (1:7). Paul does not abolish authority; he sets standards for it.

A textual note. A few Western manuscripts read “this is a human saying”. “Trustworthy” is far better attested.

On a Tuesday. If you feel drawn to serve as an elder, that desire is good. Let others test your character.
verseByVerse.note: “Overseer” and “elder” appear to be two names for the same office.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So an overseer must be above reproach, faithful to his wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable and able to teach.

Above reproach. Nothing to take hold of. Not sinless, which would empty every pulpit.

The husband of one wife. A “one-woman man”. Not “must be married” (Paul was single); not “never remarried after being widowed” (Paul advises young widows to remarry, 5:14). Most likely: faithful to his wife. A man divorced long ago, before conversion or as the innocent party, may qualify if his life is now above reproach; the church must judge with care. The qualification assumes elders are men (2:12).

Self-controlled, respectable. A man in possession of his judgement, whose life is not chaotic.

Hospitable. Inns were dangerous; travelling Christians relied on homes. His family bears the cost of his office.

Able to teach. The only skill among some fifteen requirements. Churches that choose leaders for gifting or platform have inverted Paul’s proportions.

verseByVerse.quote: not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not be a heavy drinker or violent, but gentle; not quarrelsome, and not a lover of money.

Drunkard. One who lingers by the wine. Not a ban on wine (5:23), but on drink governing a man’s evenings.

Not violent but gentle. Not a striker. Instead, epieikēs: the man who does not insist on the last inch of his rights.

Not quarrelsome. Ephesus might seem to need someone who could out-argue the false teachers. Paul disqualifies the man who enjoys the fight, however right he is.

Not a lover of money. A man who loves money will eventually be bought (6:5, 10).

Invisible for years. Drink, temper, quarrelling and money are ways of handling pressure badly, and a congregation cannot see them quickly. You can judge a sermon in twenty minutes; character takes years.

On a Tuesday. Which of these four shows up in you when you are under pressure?

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must manage his own household well, with children who respect and obey him. If a man does not know how to manage his own household, how can he take care of God’s church?

Lesser to greater. Home and church are the same kind of thing: households (v. 15).

Care for. For the church Paul changes the verb: not “manage” but “care for”, the word for the Samaritan’s care (Luke 10:34–35).

With dignity. Order without harshness. A home ruled by fear fails the spirit of this, and the violent man is already excluded (v. 3).

What it does not mean. Not a guarantee that a good father’s children will all believe. Godly parents have watched children walk away since Genesis. Paul means whether the home under his charge is visibly cared for or visibly out of control.

On a Tuesday. Your real character is known at home. No one sustains a performance in front of people who see him tired.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not be a new believer, or he may become proud and fall under the same judgment as the devil. He must also have a good reputation with outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the devil’s trap.

Recent convert. Neophytos, newly planted. Promoting him early may not honour him but endanger him.

Puffed up. Swollen with air. The devil’s condemnation is probably the judgment he incurred for pride.

A church in a hurry. A shortage of leaders is no reason to promote early, because the cost falls on the man.

Outsiders. Non-Christians get a say. Not approval of his beliefs, but no grounds to call him dishonest, cruel or unreliable.

The snare. A leader with a bad reputation outside is already trapped; everything he says about Christ is discounted.

On a Tuesday. What would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deacons likewise must be worthy of respect, honest in speech, not heavy drinkers or greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, and must first be tested, then serve if they prove blameless. The women likewise must be respected, not slanderers, sober and faithful in everything. Deacons must be faithful to their wives and manage their children and households well. Those who serve well gain good standing and great confidence in the faith in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

The gynaikas of verse 11 may be deacons' wives (so the ESV) or women serving as deacons (cf. Phoebe, Rom 16:1). The passage does not settle it; the standard of character is the same either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Missing from the deacons' list is ‘able to teach’: they serve rather than teach, under standards just as demanding.

Now: Test first, then appoint (v.10) — the order most churches reverse, to their cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, deacons must be worthy of respect, sincere in speech, not given to much wine, and not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold to the deep truths of the faith with a clear conscience. They must first be tested, and then, if there is nothing against them, let them serve as deacons.

Deacons. Diakonos, servant, probably growing from Acts 6, where seven handled food so the apostles could pray and preach.

What is missing. “Able to teach”. Deacons serve rather than teach, under standards of character just as high.

Not double-tongued. Men moving between households hear everyone’s business. Repeating it destroys the trust the job runs on.

Not greedy. Deacons handled money for the poor, often with no one checking.

A clear conscience. They need not expound the faith, but must hold it with nothing unresolved.

Tested first. Dokimazō, proving metal, by time. Observe, then appoint. Most churches appoint and find out afterwards, and that is how many come to grief.
verseByVerse.note: Deacons (“servants”) cared for the church’s practical needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way, the women must be worthy of respect, not slanderers, but sober-minded and trustworthy in everything. A deacon must be faithful to his wife and manage his children and household well. Those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing and great confidence in their faith in Christ Jesus.

Wives or women deacons? Gynaikas can mean either, and there is no “their” in the Greek. The ESV reads “their wives”, since v. 12 returns to the men. Others read “women deacons”: “likewise” introduces each new group (vv. 8, 11), the qualities match the deacons’ own, there is no parallel verse about elders’ wives, and Phoebe was a diakonos (Romans 16:1).

A verdict. The second is somewhat more likely. Many complementarian churches appoint women deacons, since the office is service, not the elders’ teaching and ruling. Others do not. The standard of character is the same either way.

Not slanderers. Diaboloi, the devil’s own name. Careless talk about people is given his title.

Confidence. Parrhēsia, freedom to speak. Not promotion, but assurance. Years of quietly carrying food to widows produce a settledness study alone does not.

On a Tuesday. Serving well does something to the server. Volunteer for the job nobody notices.
verseByVerse.note: “Their wives” may also be translated “women,” that is, women deacons; the Greek can mean either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul hopes to come soon, but writes in case he is delayed, so they will know how people should behave in God’s household, the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. Great indeed is the mystery of godliness: he appeared in a body, was vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, and taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress

The church does not create the truth; it holds it up where it can be seen (v.15). And the hymn of verse 16 is six passive lines — God does all of it — from ‘manifested in the flesh’ to ‘taken up in glory’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a city of Artemis's hundred-odd columns, house churches are called the pillar of the truth.

Now: The chapter's rules about wine, money and reputation exist so that the pillar stands straight and the mystery of godliness can be seen from the street.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing so that, if I am delayed, you will know how people should conduct themselves in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.

If I delay. The letter exists because of a contingency, like much of Scripture.

Household. The extended household of that world: kin, servants, dependants, an order and a head. The church is that, and it is God’s.

The living God. Pointed in Ephesus, whose great temple held an image that could not move.

Pillar and buttress. Artemis’s temple had over a hundred columns, sixty feet high. Paul applies the vocabulary to house churches.

The right way round. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The church does not create or authenticate the truth (as Roman Catholic teaching on the church’s magisterium can imply); it holds up the truth that stands in Scripture.

On a Tuesday. Your church is not mainly a service provider or community centre. It holds up the truth about God in your town. Help it stand straight.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can deny how great the mystery of godliness is: He appeared in a body, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed on in the world, and was taken up in glory.

A hymn. Six lines, all passive. Christ is the subject; God does it all.

Manifested in the flesh. He existed before he appeared, and appeared in real flesh: truly God, truly man.

Vindicated. Condemned by Rome; declared in the right by the Spirit in the resurrection.

Seen by angels. At every hinge of his life, and they long to look into it (1 Peter 1:12).

Proclaimed, believed. The least likely lines. A crucified provincial announced to the empire, and believed. The church in Ephesus was proof.

Taken up. The ascension: where he now is.

A textual note. Most later manuscripts read “God was manifested in the flesh” (KJV). The earliest read “He who”. In Greek the abbreviation for “God” and the word “who” differ by two small strokes, and a scribe could easily turn one into the other. “Who” is very likely original. The deity of Christ does not hang on this verse, which in either form describes the pre-existent one coming in flesh.

For worship. This is what the rules about wine and money are for: so the world can see him.
verseByVerse.note: Probably an early Christian hymn or creed, with six lines in three pairs. “He” is literally “Who” in Greek; some manuscripts read “God,” others “Which” (ESV note).
