4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
The Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, following teachers whose consciences are seared and who forbid marriage and certain foods. Paul answers with creation: everything God made is good and to be received with thanks, made holy by God’s word and prayer.

Then he turns to Timothy. Refuse silly myths and train yourself for godliness, which, unlike bodily training, pays out in this life and the next. Do not let anyone despise your youth; be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Give yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching. Let your progress be seen. Watch your life and your doctrine closely, for in this way God will save you and your hearers.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit clearly says that in later times some will abandon the faith and follow deceiving spirits and the teachings of demons, through hypocritical liars whose consciences are seared. They forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods God created to be received with thanks by believers who know the truth. For everything God created is good, and nothing should be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, because it is made holy by God’s word and prayer.
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The Ephesian error was ascetic — impressive for what it gave up — and Paul answers it not by negotiating but with Genesis 1: everything God made is good, created to be received with thanksgiving (vv.3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Seared consciences are made one over-ruling at a time, through ordinary men saying what they know to be untrue (v.2).

Now: Grace at the table sanctifies a common meal (v.5): neither refuse the gift nor grab it, but take it and say thank you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit clearly says that in later times some will abandon the faith and follow deceiving spirits and things taught by demons. These teachings come through hypocritical liars, whose consciences have been seared as with a hot iron.

Expressly. In so many words: a revealed warning, perhaps through prophets or Jesus’ own teaching.

Later times. Already begun. Paul describes Ephesus.

Demons behind it. False teaching is not merely a clever man reasoning badly; there is a source behind the visible one.

Through ordinary liars. No spectacle. Men saying what they know is untrue, in a normal voice, at a meeting.

Seared. Branded. Scar tissue does not feel. A conscience is deadened one small over-ruling at a time (1:19), and at the end it does not hurt.

On a Tuesday. If something you once felt guilty about no longer bothers you, ask whether you changed your mind or your nerve died.

verseByVerse.quote: who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They forbid people to marry and order them to abstain from certain foods, which God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.

Restriction, not licence. We expect false teaching to be permissive. This was ascetic, impressive for what it gave up. That has been at least as common in church history.

Behind it. The idea that matter is the problem and holiness means escaping the body (compare Colossians 2:21). Marriage and food, the most bodily things, had to go.

God created. Paul goes straight to creation. Refusing the gift is not superior spirituality; it insults the Giver. They were made to be received.

Clerical celibacy? The Reformers applied this verse to compulsory celibacy for priests. Singleness freely chosen for the kingdom is good (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7:7). A rule forbidding ministers to marry is not. Likewise, a Christian may avoid meat for health or conscience; teaching that holiness requires it is wrong.

Those who know the truth. Unbelievers eat and marry; they cannot receive them as gifts, because they do not know whom to thank.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God created is good, and nothing should be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, because it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.

Good. Genesis 1’s verdict, never withdrawn. The fall damaged the world’s use, not its origin.

What it does not mean. Not that anything goes. Paul speaks of created gifts such as food and marriage, not of sin. Drunkenness misuses wine; adultery misuses sex.

With thanksgiving. Gratitude turns eating into worship. The line is not between things but between ways of receiving them.

The word of God and prayer. Probably Scripture’s verdict that it is good, and grace before meals.

Saying grace. The most routine Christian habit, done on autopilot, is given priestly weight. It sets a common meal apart.

On a Tuesday. Neither refuse the gift nor grab it. Take it and say thank you, at the very moment you are most likely to forget God: when you are enjoying something.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By teaching these things Timothy will be a good servant of Christ, nourished on sound doctrine. He must refuse godless myths and train himself for godliness, which, unlike bodily training, is valuable in every way, for this life and the next. This saying is trustworthy: we work and strive because we hope in the living God, the Saviour of all people, especially of believers. Let no one despise his youth; he must be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. He must devote himself to public Scripture reading, exhortation and teaching, and not neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him. He must give himself to these things so his progress is seen, watching his life and doctrine closely.
verseByVerse.theology:
Godliness Is Trained For

Godliness is trained for like a body, by repetition (v.7), and unlike bodily training its results survive the body — with value for this life as well as the next (v.8). God is Saviour of all as their preserver, and especially of believers (v.10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Public reading of Scripture came first (v.13) in a church where few could read: read, explain, apply.

Now: A young leader earns respect by being an example where nobody is watching (v.12), and a minister whose progress is visible (v.15) teaches his people that growth does not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you teach these things to the believers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith and the sound teaching you have followed. Have nothing to do with godless myths and old wives’ tales. Instead, train yourself to be godly.

A good servant. Diakonos. Not by innovating, but by serving up what he was given.

Being nourished. Present tense. A minister who stops being fed will soon have nothing to serve.

Old-womanish myths. Deliberately dismissive. Some error deserves careful answer; some deserves to be walked past. Arguing can concede that a thing is worth arguing about.

Train. Gymnaze, the gymnasium word. Godliness is not a temperament some are born with; it is trained for by repeating unremarkable things long after they stop being interesting.

On a Tuesday. Pick one spiritual discipline (a set time of prayer, a Bible plan, a weekly fast) and keep at it when you do not feel like it.

verseByVerse.quote: for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Physical training has some value, but godliness has value in every way, because it holds promise both for this life and for the life to come.

Some value. A real concession. Paul has just defended food and marriage; he does not despise the body. Go to the gym.

Scope. Bodily training helps a little, for a while. Even the strongest body is on a schedule. Godliness is the only training whose results outlast the body.

This life too. Not a religion that pays only after death. Self-control beats being ruled by appetite; a clear conscience sleeps better; love is better company than resentment.

What it does not mean. Not that godliness brings wealth (6:5). Its present value is a better life, not a richer one.

Encouragement. Nobody changes a body by one decision. The soul works the same way. Progress does not depend on inspiration.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This saying is trustworthy and deserves full acceptance. That is why we work hard and struggle, because we have put our hope in the living God, who is the Saviour of all people, and especially of those who believe.

Toil and strive. Labour to exhaustion; contend in the arena. Paul puts himself in the gym.

Hope, not duty. The fuel is expectation, in a God who is alive, unlike Artemis down the road.

Saviour of all? Not universal salvation; the chapter opened with people abandoning the faith. Some read “all kinds of people” again. The likelier sense uses the breadth of “saviour”: God preserves and sustains every living person (Matthew 5:45; Acts 17:25), and in the full and eternal sense saves those who believe.

One generosity, two depths. Fitting after Paul’s defence of creation: the God who feeds everyone is the God who saves believers.

For worship. Every breath an unbeliever draws is a mercy from the God he ignores. So is yours.

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Command and teach these things. Do not let anyone look down on you because you are young, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith and in purity.

Command. Stronger than suggest, because the instructions were never Timothy’s own.

Youth. Probably in his thirties: young in a culture that gave authority to age, with older men who wanted his role.

Not “assert yourself”. Paul does not tell him to fight for respect, or the church to give it. He tells him to give contempt nothing to feed on.

Example. Typos, the stamp. Authority displayed, not claimed.

Five areas. From the most visible (speech) to the least (purity), and the least visible is where it is decided.

On a Tuesday. Young Christians: you do not need to be older to be an example. Older Christians: do not despise the young leader whose life is worth copying.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was probably in his thirties — young for a church leader in that culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until I come, give your attention to the public reading of Scripture, to preaching and to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you received through prophecy when the elders laid their hands on you.

Public reading first. Most could not read, and copies were scarce. Hearing the Bible meant someone reading it aloud. Before explanation, the text itself.

Read, exhort, teach. Read, apply, explain: Christian ministry in three words.

On a Tuesday. If your church reads only a verse or two before the sermon, ask whether it could read more. Scripture read aloud is itself ministry.

Do not neglect. A gift can be possessed and wasted, left in a drawer.

The laying on of hands. The elders publicly recognised and set Timothy apart for a gift the Spirit had given. Roman Catholic and Orthodox teaching regards ordination as a sacrament conveying grace. Here the act recognises and commissions; the gift is the Spirit’s.

A council. Plural. When the job goes badly, remember that a body of men publicly stood with you.

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Practise these things and give yourself wholly to them, so that everyone can see your progress. Watch your life and your teaching closely. Keep at it, because by doing so you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

Immerse yourself. Literally “be in these things”. Live there.

Progress. Prokopē, cutting a road ahead. Visible: the congregation should see a better man than five years ago. A leader who never visibly grows teaches that growth stops.

Yourself first. Then the teaching. A man can guard his theology while his character comes apart (1:19). But both: character without sound teaching helps no one; sound teaching from a corrupt man is a weapon.

Save yourself and your hearers. No minister saves anyone; there is one mediator (2:5). God saves through means, including a man who keeps watching himself and teaching truly. Perseverance in faith is how salvation is kept, by God’s power.

On a Tuesday. Watch yourself: what you read, watch and think about when no one is checking.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons,<sup>2</sup>through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,<sup>3</sup>who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.<sup>4</sup>For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving,<sup>5</sup>for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.<sup>6</sup>If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed.<sup>7</sup>Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;<sup>8</sup>for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.<sup>9</sup>The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance.<sup>10</sup>For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.<sup>11</sup>Command and teach these things.<sup>12</sup>Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.<sup>13</sup>Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching.<sup>14</sup>Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.<sup>15</sup>Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress.<sup>16</sup>Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.

5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
The church is a family, and Paul tells Timothy how to treat its members: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Then two practical matters. Widows: the church must support those truly alone, but families must first care for their own, and a Christian who neglects his relatives “has denied the faith”. Younger widows should remarry rather than take a vow they may not keep.

Elders: those who lead well, especially in preaching, should be paid generously, and Paul quotes a saying of Jesus as Scripture. Accusations against elders need two or three witnesses, but elders who persist in sin are rebuked publicly. Appoint slowly, judge without favouritism, and remember that both hidden sins and hidden goodness will come to light.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not rebuke an older man harshly but appeal to him as a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with complete purity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as Household, in Practice

This is 3:15 turned into method: treat people as what they actually are — fathers, brothers, mothers, sisters — which rules out both harshness and a deference that never says anything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young leader not taken seriously is tempted to be harsher than the case requires (4:12).

Now: ‘As sisters, in all purity’ gives a relationship rather than a rulebook as the safeguard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not rebuke an older man harshly, but appeal to him as you would to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.

Not harshly. To strike with words. Older men may need correcting, but not like that. A young leader not taken seriously (4:12) is tempted to compensate by being sharper than the case needs.

A family. The church as God’s household (3:15), in practice. You correct your father carefully and never in public; you are frank with a brother. It rules out both harshness and a deference that never says anything.

In all purity. Added only for younger women. A realist’s word to a young unmarried minister: many ministries have been destroyed here.

As sisters. The safeguard is a relationship, not a rulebook. A man already knows what is unthinkable with his sister. It protects them both without treating half the church as a hazard.

On a Tuesday. Think of the hardest person in your church. How would you speak to them if they were family? They are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Honour and support widows who are truly in need. If a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to care for their own family and repay their parents, which pleases God. The widow who is truly alone hopes in God and prays night and day; the one who lives for pleasure is dead while she lives. Anyone who does not provide for his relatives has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. A widow should be put on the list if she is over sixty, was faithful to her husband, and is known for good works. Younger widows should not be enrolled; they may want to remarry and break their pledge, and idleness leads to gossip. Better that they marry and run their homes. Believing families should care for their own widows, so the church can help those truly alone.
verseByVerse.theology:
Family First, and Why

To neglect one's own relatives is to deny the faith and fall below the decency of unbelievers (v.8); caring for an ageing parent is not a lesser duty but where godliness is practised (v.4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The enrolled widows were intercessors (v.5), and their credentials were a lifetime of unrecorded service (v.10).

Now: Paul's remedy for the dangers of verses 11–13 is not more restriction but ordinary life (v.14).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honour widows who are truly in need. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to put their faith into practice by caring for their own family and repaying their parents, because this pleases God.

Honour. Including money, as in v. 17. This is the church’s welfare list.

A widow then. No state support, few respectable ways to earn, often no property. Without family she was destitute. God defends the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18); the church’s first crisis was about widows (Acts 6:1).

Truly widows. Limited funds must reach the genuinely alone.

Family first. The church is not the first line of support. Children repay a debt.

Where godliness is. Caring for an ageing mother is not a secular duty keeping you from spiritual things. It is godliness. The opposite of the “Corban” dodge Jesus condemned (Mark 7:9–13).

On a Tuesday. Phone your parents. If they are old, ask what they need.

verseByVerse.quote: She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A widow who is truly in need, left completely alone, puts her hope in God and keeps praying night and day. But the widow who lives for pleasure is dead even while she lives.

Alone. Not only bereaved but with no one to turn to.

Night and day. Like Anna in the temple (Luke 2:37). The church is not only giving charity; it is supporting intercessors. A congregation that keeps its widows is buying prayer it could not otherwise afford.

Self-indulgent. Resources, no dependants, freedom spent on pleasure.

Dead while she lives. Present tense, like Sardis (Revelation 3:1).

Two women. Both widowed, both with time. One prays and is alive; the other spends it on herself and has not noticed she is dead.

On a Tuesday. Retired? What you do with unstructured time reveals you. Spend some of it praying for your church.

verseByVerse.quote: Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give these instructions too, so that no one may be open to blame. Anyone who does not provide for his relatives, and especially his own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

Without reproach. The overseer’s word (3:2), now for families caring for their own. A watching city judges Christian homes.

Denied the faith. Peter’s verb in the courtyard. A man can recite the creed and, by leaving his mother destitute, deny every word.

Worse than an unbeliever. Pagans looked after their own. Neglect falls below ordinary decency.

What it does not mean. It does not settle every hard case: estrangement for grave reasons, relatives no money can help, carers at the end of their strength. Paul means those who could and do not, and have arranged their religion so as not to notice.

On a Tuesday. Spirituality here is measured not by devotion or ministry, but by whether your relatives have what they need.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A widow may be put on the list if she is at least sixty years old, was faithful to her husband, and is known for good works: raising children, showing hospitality, washing the feet of God’s people, helping those in trouble, and devoting herself to every kind of good work.

Enrolled. An official list, probably with duties.

Sixty. Past likely remarriage and earning: where long-term dependence begins.

Wife of one husband. A faithful wife. Not excluding remarriage after widowhood, since Paul urges younger widows to remarry (v. 14).

Washed feet. The lowest household job, which Jesus did (John 13:5).

Unrecorded credentials. Not one item is public. She is enrolled for a lifetime of things nobody wrote down. Before she needed help, she gave it.

On a Tuesday. The church owes its quiet servants. Find out who in your church is now in need after years of helping others.
verseByVerse.note: There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in turn served it.

verseByVerse.quote: But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But do not put younger widows on the list. When their desires draw them away from their dedication to Christ, they want to marry, and so bring judgment on themselves for breaking their first pledge. They also learn to be idle, going from house to house, and become gossips and busybodies, saying things they should not.

Not against remarriage. Paul urges it in v. 14.

Their former pledge. Most likely a commitment made on joining the list, to remain unmarried in the church’s service. Breaking it is the problem, not marrying.

Pastoral realism. Do not ask a woman in her twenties to bind herself for life. Most will not manage it, and the failure will damage them.

They learn. The arrangement teaches it. A stipend with no work or structure fills days somehow, often with other people’s business (2 Thessalonians 3:11).

The general lesson. Not about women or widows. Idleness is never neutral. Remove someone’s proper work and the energy goes into other people’s affairs.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I want younger widows to marry, have children, manage their homes, and give the enemy no opportunity to slander us. Some have already turned away to follow Satan. If any believing woman has widows in her family, she should help them, so the church is not burdened and can help widows who are truly alone.

Marry. Not only allowed; preferred. Against teachers who forbade marriage (4:3), Paul’s cure is ordinary life.

Manage their households. Literally “rule the house”: a real sphere of authority.

No occasion. The church is watched from the street (3:7).

Already. Not hypothetical. Some had gone off the road.

The arithmetic of love. Every family that supports its own frees the church to help those with no one.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts read “any believing man or woman” (KJV). The shorter “believing woman” is earlier, and harder, so more likely original. The duty of v. 8 is not men’s alone.

Today. Few churches keep a widows’ list, but the principle stands: real need, met first by family, then by the church. Families may not hand their duty to the church or the state.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elders who lead well deserve double honour, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it treads the grain,” and, “The worker deserves his wages.” Do not accept an accusation against an elder without two or three witnesses. Those who keep sinning should be rebuked publicly, so others will fear. Keep these rules without prejudice or favouritism, before God, Christ and the chosen angels. Do not ordain anyone hastily, or share in others’ sins; keep yourself pure. Take a little wine for your stomach. Some sins are obvious; others show up later. So too good works: even hidden ones cannot stay hidden.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gospel Quoted as Scripture

Verse 18 introduces both Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying of Jesus recorded at Luke 10:7 with ‘the Scripture says’ — among the earliest signs that the written words of Jesus were already counted as Scripture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Elders are hard to accuse (v.19) and hard to hide behind (v.20); a church needs both verses.

Now: Verse 23 shows Paul correcting a good man's over-scrupulous mistake, and verse 25 promises that unrecorded goodness cannot stay hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders who lead the church well should be considered worthy of double honour, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. For Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker deserves his wages.”

Honour means pay. Both quotations are about paying workers.

Double. Generous, not grudging.

Especially. Implies some elders taught and some did not. Presbyterians see here teaching and ruling elders; Baptists and others usually see one office with differing labours. The text allows either.

Labour. Kopiaō, work to exhaustion. Preaching is not restful.

The ox. Deuteronomy 25:4, applied to people (1 Corinthians 9:9).

“The Scripture says.” The second quotation is Jesus’ saying in Luke 10:7. Paul calls both Scripture: one of the earliest signs that Jesus’ written words already stood with the Old Testament (compare 2 Peter 3:16).

On a Tuesday. Is your church paying its pastor enough to live without anxiety? Ask.
verseByVerse.note: The two sayings come from Deuteronomy and from Jesus’ words as recorded in Luke — a sign that the Gospels were already being received as Scripture.

parallels.desc: You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not accept an accusation against an elder unless it is supported by two or three witnesses. But those elders who keep on sinning should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will be afraid.

Two or three witnesses. Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16. A public man is a target; accusations cost the accuser nothing. Do not even open proceedings on one person’s word.

Not a shield. Those who persist, after private dealing, are rebuked publicly.

Against instinct. Churches usually protect the institution: settle quietly, move the man on. Paul says public office, public correction, so others fear.

Both verses. Hard to accuse; hard to hide behind. Keep only the first and leaders become untouchable; keep only the second and any grievance ruins a man.

What it does not mean. The witness rule is about church discipline. It never means a church may ignore a crime or refuse to report abuse to the authorities.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before God, Christ Jesus and the chosen angels, I solemnly charge you to keep these instructions without prejudging anyone and without showing favouritism.

Sworn in. The most solemn sentence in the letter.

Elect angels. Watchers of church life (1 Corinthians 11:10; 1 Peter 1:12), distinguished from the fallen. A courtroom with an unseen gallery.

Prejudging, partiality. Deciding in advance; leaning one way. Timothy will have friends and opponents among the elders, and will know before hearing a charge which way he wants it to go.

The test. Rules are easy when the accused is a stranger. The hard case is when you already know whose side you are on. Paul’s answer is not better procedure, but who is watching.

On a Tuesday. In any dispute (at work, in your family), notice who you want to be right before you hear the facts.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be hasty in laying hands on anyone to appoint them, and do not share in other people’s sins. Keep yourself pure.

Laying on of hands. Appointment to office (4:14).

Do not be hasty. As at 3:6. Ephesus needed leaders, and the pressure to fill posts was great.

Share in sins. Whoever appoints carelessly is implicated in what the appointed man later does. He cannot say he could not have known, since testing (3:10) would often have shown him.

Keep yourself pure. A great deal of holiness is kept or lost in decisions that look merely procedural.

On a Tuesday. Writing a reference or recommending someone? You share responsibility. Be honest.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop drinking only water. Use a little wine for your stomach and because you are often ill.

A window into a friendship. Medical advice in the middle of instructions on discipline.

Two facts. Timothy was often ill, and he drank only water, risky when supplies were unsafe and wine was used to purify them.

Why? Probably on principle: against ascetics (4:3), and wanting to be above reproach (3:3), he went teetotal and made himself ill.

A little, for your stomach. Neither a licence nor a prohibition.

Why not heal him? Even Paul, through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12), did not heal at will, and here prescribes a remedy. Illness is not always a sign of sin or weak faith, and using medicine is no lack of trust.

For the scrupulous. A good man’s mistake: trying to be blameless and overshooting into harm. Paul does not praise the rigour. He tells him to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some people’s sins are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; others’ sins show up later. In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even those that are not cannot stay hidden for ever.

Conspicuous sins. They walk ahead like heralds; no examination needed.

Later. Others catch up eventually.

Honest. After careful procedure (3:10; 5:19, 22), Paul admits it will not catch everything. He does not respond by adding more rules.

Nothing stays hidden. If not now, then at judgment. So haste is unnecessary: waiting does not risk the truth never emerging.

The kinder half. The same law runs for goodness. The widow’s unrecorded lifetime (v. 10) is not lost.

On a Tuesday. If your faithfulness has gone unnoticed, or someone else got the credit, both ledgers are being kept, and both will be read out.

Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.<sup>17</sup>Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.<sup>18</sup>For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."<sup>19</sup>Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>20</sup>As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.<sup>21</sup>In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.<sup>22</sup>Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.<sup>23</sup>No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.<sup>24</sup>The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later.<sup>25</sup>So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.

6.title: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain
6.overview:
The last chapter ties the letter together. Slaves are to honour their masters, so that God’s name is not slandered. Then the root of the false teaching is exposed: these men thought godliness was a way to make money. Paul answers that “godliness with contentment is great gain”, since we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

Timothy, the man of God, must flee all this and pursue righteousness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness, fighting the good fight until Christ appears, the King of kings who dwells in unapproachable light. The rich are not told to give everything away, but to hope in God, who gives richly for enjoyment, and to be rich in good works. Finally: guard the deposit, and grace be with you all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Slaves should regard their masters as worthy of full respect, so that God’s name and the teaching are not slandered. Those with believing masters should not show less respect because they are brothers, but serve them even better, because those who benefit are fellow believers, dearly loved.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Paul Does and Does Not Say

Paul gives slaves a reason for their conduct that has nothing to do with their masters' rights — the honour of God's name (v.1) — and sets it beside his condemnation of slave-trading (1:10) and his plea for Onesimus (Philem 16): a principle planted inside the institution that would in time dissolve it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Equality in Christ, Paul says, should make a slave serve a believing master better, not worse (v.2).

Now: The strategy took far too long, and Christians defended slavery with verses like this while ignoring 1:10 — yet abolition came largely from people arguing from this book.

verseByVerse.quote: Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who are slaves should consider their masters worthy of full respect, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be slandered. Those whose masters are believers should not show them less respect because they are brothers. Instead, they should serve them even better, because those who benefit from their work are believers and dearly loved.

The scale. Perhaps a third of Ephesus was enslaved, and some slaves had Christian masters. A call for immediate revolt would have been crushed, and the church with it.

A new reason. Not “your master deserves it”, but “God’s name is in your hands”. A slave is a witness.

Brothers. Some reasoned that equality in Christ cancelled the arrangement. Paul affirms the equality (“beloved”) but says it should make service better, not worse.

Does the Bible approve slavery? No. Paul condemns slave-trading (1:10), tells masters they have a Master (Ephesians 6:9), urges slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and sends Onesimus back as a brother (Philemon 16). He planted a principle that would dissolve the institution.

Honestly. It took far too long, and Christians quoted verses like this while ignoring 1:10. But abolition came largely from people arguing from this book.

On a Tuesday. Employees with Christian bosses: do not take advantage of the relationship. Work better.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Anyone who teaches something different and rejects the sound words of the Lord Jesus is proud and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy, which produces envy, strife, slander, suspicion and constant friction among people who think godliness is a way to get rich. But godliness with contentment is great gain. We brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out; with food and clothing we will be content. Those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a trap, into foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and some, craving it, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Root Beneath the Quarrels

Beneath the Ephesian error was a business — ‘godliness is a means of gain’ (v.5) — and its fruit was relational damage rather than doctrinal error (v.4). The love of money, a root of all kinds of evils (v.10), enables every sin rather than having one of its own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul grants the false teachers their word ‘gain’ and attaches it to contentment (v.6).

Now: Verse 9 warns those who desire to be rich — a condition available at every income.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone teaches something different and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that leads to godliness, he is conceited and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy appetite for controversy and quarrels about words. These produce envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions and constant friction among people whose minds are corrupt and who have lost the truth, thinking that godliness is a way to get rich.

The standard. Sound, healthy words, tested by whether they produce godliness (1:5).

Puffed up, understanding nothing. Maximum self-regard, zero comprehension. They often travel together.

Diseased craving. The opposite of “sound”. He does not tolerate argument; he needs it.

The fruit. Five words, none a doctrinal error: all relational damage. A church where people suspect each other has a teaching problem, whatever its statement of faith.

The root. Godliness as gain. Under the genealogies was a business.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts add “from such withdraw yourself” (KJV). It is absent from the earliest copies.

On a Tuesday. Of any teacher whose doctrine seems off, ask not only “Is it true?” but “What does he get out of it?”

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But godliness with contentment is great gain. We brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. So if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that.

Their word, turned. There is gain, but attached to contentment.

Contentment. Autarkeia, the Stoic word, refilled: not needing nothing, but having enough because of who supplies you (Philippians 4:11–13).

Nothing in, nothing out. Job 1:21; Ecclesiastes 5:15. Anyone can verify it; no one has disproved it. Possessions are held for the middle stretch only.

Food and clothing. The word can include shelter. Paul sets the bar at survival.

What it does not mean. Not that having more is wrong. God gives “everything to enjoy” (v. 17). Everything above food and clothing is surplus, and a Christian should know it.

A textual note. Many later manuscripts insert “and it is certain” before “we can take nothing out” (KJV). The shorter text is earlier.

On a Tuesday. Did contentment arrive with your last pay rise? If not, it will not come with the next.

parallels.desc: Naked I came from my mother's womb

verseByVerse.quote: But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But people who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.

Desire, not wealth. The warning is to those who want to be rich, a condition available at every income. The rich get separate instructions (v. 17).

The descent. Fall into a snare; desires arrive in company; then ruin, like a ship dragged under.

Three corrections. Not money, but the love of it. Not the root, but a root; pride and lust need no money. Not all evil, but all kinds: it has no characteristic sin because it enables every sin.

Wandered. Nobody sets out to leave Christ for money. They drift while looking at something else.

Pierced themselves. Self-inflicted, and the griefs come to the one who got what he wanted.

The prosperity gospel. Teaching that faith guarantees wealth is exactly what Paul condemns in v. 5.

On a Tuesday. Give something away this week, to loosen money’s grip.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But Timothy, as a man of God, must flee these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness. He must fight the good fight of the faith and take hold of eternal life, to which he was called when he made his good confession before many witnesses. Before God, who gives life to everything, and Christ Jesus, who made the good confession before Pontius Pilate, Paul charges him to keep the command spotless until Christ appears. God will bring that about at the right time: the blessed and only Ruler, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone is immortal and lives in unapproachable light, whom no one has seen or can see. To him be honour and eternal power.
verseByVerse.theology:
Titles Thrown at Idols

‘Only Sovereign’, ‘King of kings and Lord of lords’, ‘who alone has immortality’ (vv.15–16) are aimed at Artemis and the emperor; and the God who dwells in unapproachable light is reached only through the one mediator (2:5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy confessed Christ among friends; Jesus confessed before Pilate, who could kill him (vv.12–13).

Now: Flee and pursue (v.11): some temptations must simply be run from, and a man who only avoids will eventually be caught.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, man of God, run from all this, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness.

Man of God. The prophets’ title: Moses, Samuel, Elijah. Laid on a struggling young minister.

Flee. As Joseph ran from Potiphar’s wife (Genesis 39:12). Some temptations are not to be reasoned with. A man who stays to test his strength has decided how it ends.

Pursue. A hunter’s verb. Fleeing alone leaves a vacuum.

Three pairs. Righteousness and godliness (towards people, towards God). Faith and love (1:5). Endurance and gentleness: immovable and unaggravated at once, holding ground without becoming like those pushing you.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you need to run from, and the thing you will run towards instead.
verseByVerse.note: “Man of God” is an Old Testament title for prophets such as Moses, Samuel and Elijah.

verseByVerse.quote: Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made your good confession in front of many witnesses.

Fight. Agōnizou, the arena word behind “agony”. The good fight of the faith: the contest over the deposit itself (v. 20).

Take hold. Seize and keep hold. Timothy has eternal life as a gift and is told to grip it (Philippians 2:12–13). Secure possession, and the grip still commanded.

The good confession. Probably his baptism or commissioning. Feelings about ministry come and go; the fact that you confessed Christ before witnesses does not. Put your weight on it.

On a Tuesday. Remember your baptism. On the days nothing feels steady, that is a fixed point.
verseByVerse.note: The “good confession” was probably made at Timothy’s baptism or ordination.

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before God, who gives life to everything, and before Christ Jesus, who made the good confession when he testified before Pontius Pilate, I charge you to keep this command without stain or blame until our Lord Jesus Christ appears.

The witnesses. God, who gives life: what a man needs to remember if the charge may cost his. Christ, who told the truth to a governor who could kill him, and did.

Two confessions. Timothy’s among friends; Jesus’ before a hostile ruler. The same act, with the price attached.

Pontius Pilate. A name from Roman records. The faith is not a philosophy but something that happened at a particular hour.

The commandment. Most likely the whole deposit of faith (v. 20).

Unstained. A man’s life can stain the message he carries.

Until the appearing. The assignment has one end date, and it is not in Timothy’s diary.

verseByVerse.quote: which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will bring this about at the right time. He is the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone is immortal and who lives in light no one can approach, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honour and eternal power. Amen.

The proper time. Kairos. No one hurries it or delays it.

Stones thrown at idols. “Only Sovereign”, in a city of Artemis and emperor-worship. “King of kings”: imperial vocabulary, given to someone else.

Alone has immortality. Deathless by nature. Angels and souls continue because he sustains them.

Unapproachable light. Not darkness hiding God but too much brightness (Exodus 33:20).

No technique. Against teachers selling special access: no one can get nearer by method. Which makes 2:5 astonishing: one mediator, the man Christ Jesus. The unapproachable light came out to meet us.

For worship. Read these titles aloud slowly, and bow.

parallels.desc: man shall not see me and live

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Command the rich not to be proud or to put their hope in uncertain wealth, but in God, who richly gives everything for our enjoyment. They should do good, be rich in good works, generous and willing to share, storing up a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life. Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Turn away from godless chatter and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge, which some have professed and so wandered from the faith. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guard the Deposit

The paratheke of verse 20 is property left for safekeeping, to be returned exactly as received — not developed or made more interesting — against ‘what is falsely called knowledge’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul does not tell the rich to divest but to hope in God, who gives everything to enjoy (v.17), and to get rich in good works (v.18).

Now: The closing grace is plural (v.21): after pages addressed to Timothy, Paul turns to the whole room.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Command those who are rich in this present world not to be arrogant or to put their hope in wealth, which is so uncertain, but to put their hope in God, who richly gives us everything to enjoy. Command them to do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and willing to share. In this way they will store up treasure as a firm foundation for the coming age, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.

Not “divest”. Paul does not call wealth a sin. He gives instructions for handling it.

Haughty. Money’s natural drift: persuading you that you are a different kind of person.

The uncertainty of riches. Wealth’s defining property, as a hope, is that it might not be there.

Everything to enjoy. From the man who just said food and clothing are enough. The final answer to the ascetics of chapter 4: God means us to be glad of his gifts.

Rich in good works. Rich in one currency; get rich in another.

Ready to share. Holding possessions as available to those in need.

Treasure. Matthew 6:19–20. Giving is the only investment with guaranteed returns.

Earning heaven? No. Good works are faith’s fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10), and the reward is grace. No fixed amount is set; the measure is a generous heart.

On a Tuesday. If you earn well, you are “the rich in this present age”. Set up a regular gift you will feel.

verseByVerse.quote: O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Turn away from godless chatter and the contradictory claims of what is falsely called knowledge.

O Timothy. A hand on the shoulder.

The deposit. Parathēkē, valuables left with a trustworthy man, to be returned exactly as received: not invested, improved or made more interesting.

Falsely called knowledge. Gnōsis, the word that would name the second century’s great heresy, with its secret insider knowledge. It advertises knowledge and has none.

The choice. A fixed deposit, handed on; or endless new material that sounds impressive. The second is always more exciting.

How to guard. Not by aggression (3:3; 6:4). A guard does not chase; he stays at his post, and the treasure is still there in the morning.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of the teacher who says the church has misunderstood the faith for two thousand years and he has finally found it.
verseByVerse.note: “Knowledge” may point to early forms of the teaching later called Gnosticism.

verseByVerse.quote: for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By professing it, some have wandered from the faith. Grace be with you all.

Full circle. The archer’s “swerved” of 1:6 returns. This is what the whole letter has been about.

By professing it. Claiming the knowledge committed them, and the faith had to be adjusted around their claim. Public positions take their makers where they did not intend to go.

You, plural. After addressing Timothy, Paul turns to the whole church: elders, widows, rich, slaves, would-be teachers.

A textual note. Later manuscripts read “with you” in the singular and add “Amen”. The plural is earlier and fits a letter read aloud to the church.

For worship. A demanding letter, with warnings and discipline, ends with the only thing that makes any of it possible: grace.
verseByVerse.note: “You” here is plural: the letter was meant for the whole church to hear.
